what-is-the-mern-stack: MERN = MongoDB (data), Express (API), React (screens), Node.js (runs JavaScript on the server).
A request: browser loads React, React calls the API with `fetch`, Express handles it, MongoDB returns documents, the data comes back as JSON.
One language, JavaScript, across the whole stack.
React shows, Express decides, MongoDB remembers.
set-up-your-tools-for-mern: Tools: an editor (VS Code), Node.js with npm, Git, and MongoDB (local or Atlas).
Node runs your code outside the browser. npm installs packages.
Git records every change so you can go back and share.
Keep projects in simple folders with no spaces in the names.
modern-javascript-for-mern: `const` by default, `let` when the value changes, never `var`.
Arrow functions with `map` and `filter` change lists without loops.
Destructuring: `const { title, status } = job;`. Spread copies without changing the original: `{ ...job }`.
Optional chaining `job?.company?.name` and defaults `?? 'none'` avoid crashes.
Modules: `export` shares a value, `import` uses it. Use `"type": "module"` in Node.
asynchronous-javascript-promises-async-a: Slow jobs (network, files) must not freeze JavaScript, so they run asynchronously.
A promise is a placeholder for a value that arrives later.
`await` pauses only your function. Wrap it in `try/catch` to handle failure.
`Promise.all` runs tasks at the same time.
`fetch` returns a promise. Check `response.ok`, then `await response.json()`.
Callbacks are the older way. Prefer async/await.
http-json-and-rest-basics: A request = method + path + headers + sometimes a JSON body.
GET reads, POST creates, PATCH changes, DELETE removes.
Status codes: 2xx success, 4xx the request was wrong, 5xx the server failed.
Common ones: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400, 401, 404, 500.
REST: nouns in the path (`/api/jobs/12`), verbs in the method.
plan-the-job-tracker-project: Plan before coding: what must people be able to do?
Features become screens, screens become API routes, routes decide the data.
Folders: one for the `server`, one for the `client`.
A plan costs minutes and saves hours of rewriting.
node-js-basics-modules-files-events: Node runs JavaScript on your computer, not in a browser.
Built-in modules: `fs` for files, `path` for file paths, `events` for events.
Use `path.join` so paths work on every system.
An event emitter lets one part announce something and others react.
npm-package-json-and-environment-variabl: `package.json` = name, scripts and the packages the project needs.
`npm install` reads it and fills `node_modules`. Do not commit `node_modules`.
Scripts: `npm run dev` and `npm start`. `nodemon` or `--watch` restarts on change.
Secrets and settings go in `.env`, loaded by `dotenv` into `process.env`. Never commit `.env`.
Commit `.env.example` with the names only, so others know what to fill in.
your-first-express-server-and-routes: Express checks routes from the top and runs the first match.
`res.status(200).json(data)` sends the answer and ends the request.
Order matters: put specific routes before general ones.
Try it with the browser, `curl` or a REST client.
express-middleware-json-cors-and-logging: Middleware = a function every request passes through, in order.
It must call `next()` or send a reply. Otherwise the request hangs.
`express.json()` turns the JSON body into `req.body`. Without it `req.body` is empty.
`cors` lets the browser app call this API.
A logger records method, path and time taken.
Middleware can be added to one route only.
express-routers-and-controllers: Split by responsibility so the project stays readable.
A router lists URLs and the functions that answer them.
A controller holds the logic: read input, do the work, send the reply.
Moving to MongoDB later only changes the data layer.
validation-and-error-handling-in-express: Never trust what a client sends.
Validate: check the types, keep only the allowed fields, clean the text.
One error middleware at the end sends one JSON shape for every error.
Unexpected errors become a plain 500. Details go in the log, not to the visitor.
test-your-api-with-rest-client-and-smoke: Try the routes after writing them.
Level 1: a `.http` file, Postman or `curl`, one request at a time.
Check both the status code and the body.
Level 2: a smoke script repeats all checks so you can run it after every change.
what-is-mongodb-documents-collections-at: A server holds databases, a database holds collections, a collection holds documents.
A document is a JSON-like object with an `_id`.
A collection is like a table, but documents need not have the same fields.
Atlas = MongoDB hosted for you. Or install it locally.
`mongosh` lets you try `insertOne`, `find` and `updateOne` by hand.
connect-express-to-mongodb-with-mongoose: The connection string is a secret: keep it in `.env`.
Start listening only after the database connects.
If it fails, stop with a clear message.
Common problems: wrong password, IP address not allowed in Atlas, special characters in the password.
mongoose-schemas-models-and-validation: A schema describes a document: fields, types, `required`, defaults, allowed values.
`mongoose.model('Job', schema)` gives the tool to read and write jobs.
Bad data is rejected with a `ValidationError`.
`Job.create()` or `save()` writes it to the collection.
crud-with-mongoose-in-express: Create: `Job.create` with only the allowed fields from the body (not the whole `req.body`).
Read one: `Job.findById`. A bad id gives 400, a missing job gives 404.
Update: PATCH with `runValidators: true` so the rules apply to changes too.
Translate database errors into friendly API errors.
search-filter-sort-pagination-and-indexe: The client sends search, status, sort and page in the URL.
Escape search text so it cannot be used as a regex attack.
`skip` and `limit` return one page. Send the total so the client can show page numbers.
Cap the limit so nobody asks for a million rows.
An index lets MongoDB jump to matches instead of reading every document.
mongodb-aggregation-pipeline-for-statist: An aggregation is a pipeline: each stage gets the output of the one before.
`$match` keeps the documents you want, for example the current user's jobs.
`$group` makes buckets, for example by status, and counts them.
Shape the result into a simple object for the dashboard.
Route order matters: `/stats` must come before `/:id`.
user-registration-and-password-hashing-w: Never store passwords. Store a hash.
bcrypt = one-way, adds a random salt, slow on purpose.
Check the email format and a sensible password length first.
A stolen database does not give the passwords away.
The reply never includes the hash.
A duplicate email gives a clear conflict error (409).
login-with-jwt-json-web-tokens: Login: find the user, compare the password with the stored hash using bcrypt.
Unknown email? Compare against a dummy hash anyway, so timing does not reveal which emails exist.
On success sign a JWT with a secret. It holds the user id and an expiry.
The client sends the token with later requests in the `Authorization` header.
Use the same message for every login failure.
Where the client stores the token (memory, localStorage or a cookie) is a security trade-off.
protect-routes-and-ownership-checks: The `protect` middleware reads the token from `Authorization`, verifies it and loads the user.
No token or a bad one: 401. Otherwise set `req.user` and call `next()`.
Every query includes the owner: find by id AND user.
Never take the user id from the request body.
Another person's job gives 404, as if it did not exist, so nothing is leaked.
Prove it with a test: user B cannot read or change user A's data.
express-security-basics-helmet-rate-limi: Security is several small layers, not one switch.
`helmet` adds safe headers to every reply.
Rate limit login routes so nobody can try thousands of passwords.
NoSQL injection sends objects like `{"$gt": ""}` instead of strings. Reject keys that start with `$`.
Behind a proxy set `trust proxy` so the limiter sees the real visitor address.
In production, refuse to start with a missing or weak JWT secret.
automated-api-tests-with-node-test-runne: Tests are code that checks your code. `node --test` needs no extra package.
Split `app.js` (the app) from `server.js` (listening), so tests can import the app without a real server.
Use a separate test database and clear it before each run.
Each test sends a request and checks the status and the body, including failure cases.
Run the tests before every deploy.
react-and-vite-setup-components-and-jsx: A component is a function that returns JSX. Names start with a capital letter.
Vite compiles JSX and reloads instantly while you work.
Components can contain other components, like `Header` and `JobCard`.
A Vite proxy sends `/api` calls to your Express server during development.
react-props-state-and-events: Props: inputs from the parent. They are read-only.
State: data that changes. `const [jobs, setJobs] = useState([])`.
Never change state in place. Make a new array: `[...jobs, newJob]`, `filter`, `map`.
Events: `onClick`, `onChange`. Pass the function, do not call it.
A child tells the parent by calling a function it received as a prop.
Lists need a stable `key`, the id.
react-lists-forms-and-controlled-inputs: Controlled input: state is the single source of truth. `value` shows it, `onChange` updates it.
On submit validate the state first and show clear messages next to the fields.
Every input has a `label` tied to it. It helps screen readers and makes the click area bigger.
Lists use a stable `key`, the id, not the index.
Keep state in the nearest component that needs it, or lift it up.
react-useeffect-and-fetching-data-from-y: Render first with no data and show a loading state. Then the effect starts the fetch.
The dependency list says when to run it again.
Three states: loading, error (with retry), data.
The cleanup function cancels the request, so old answers cannot overwrite new ones.
Keep all API calls in one helper file that adds the token and handles errors.
react-router-pages-links-and-params: The URL decides which page shows. React Router matches it against your routes.
A layout route draws the header once and `<Outlet />` shows the page inside it.
`useParams` reads `:id` from the URL, then load that job.
`Link` and `NavLink` change the URL without reloading.
A `*` route shows a not found page.
react-context-and-custom-hooks: Context shares data (like the signed-in user) without passing props through every level.
A provider holds the data. `useContext` reads it.
A custom hook `useAuth` hides the context behind one call.
`useJobs` keeps loading, error and reload logic in one reusable place.
react-crud-ui-create-edit-delete-with-th: Forms and buttons call the `api` helper, which adds the token and the JSON.
The server validates and changes the data, then replies.
Update the list in state only after the server confirms, using new arrays.
Show a saving state on the button. Confirm before delete.
Show a clear message when a request fails.
sign-in-and-register-pages-with-protecte: `ProtectedRoute` checks the auth context. No user: redirect to login and remember the wanted address.
After login save the token and go back to the page they wanted.
A 401 from the server signs the person out and shows the login page again.
Hiding a page in React is only a convenience. The server still checks every request.
react-dashboard-stats-filters-and-pagina: Put the search, status and page in the URL with `useSearchParams`.
The data hook watches the URL and fetches again when it changes.
The back button, reload and shared links then all work.
Debounce typing so one request is sent, not one per key.
Small focused components: list, stats, pagination.
responsive-styling-and-accessibility-in-: Mobile first: write styles for a small screen, then add `min-width` media queries.
Grid and flexible sizes let cards fill the space without fixed widths.
Visible focus rings, labels, enough colour contrast, keyboard use.
`prefers-color-scheme` gives a dark mode that follows the device.
react-performance-memo-debounce-and-code: Slowness comes from doing too much work, not from React itself.
Debounce: wait until typing stops, then send one request.
`React.memo` skips redrawing a component whose props did not change.
`lazy` loads a page only when it is visited, so the first load is smaller.
Measure first with the browser tools and the build output, then optimise.
file-upload-with-multer-and-react: React sends the file in `FormData`. It checks the size as a courtesy.
`multer` reads the upload with a size limit, one file only and an extension filter.
Read the first bytes: a text file renamed to `.pdf` is rejected and deleted.
Store the file under a random name. Only the details go in MongoDB.
Downloads go through a route that checks ownership and send the file as an attachment.
production-ready-express-logging-gracefu: Log JSON lines with path, status and time. Never log passwords or tokens.
A health check that tests the database. 503 means do not send traffic here.
On `SIGTERM`: stop new connections, finish current requests, close the database, exit.
Build indexes on purpose after a deploy. Compress text responses.
Check the logs when something looks wrong, not only when it breaks.
build-and-serve-the-react-app-from-expre: `npm run build` makes hashed static files in `client/dist`.
Express serves them. Hashed `/assets` are cached for a year. `index.html` is never cached.
`/api` goes to the API. An unknown API path is a JSON 404.
Any other GET returns `index.html`, so React Router works after a reload.
One process and one origin: no CORS needed, one thing to deploy.
deploy-a-mern-app-to-a-vps-with-pm2-ngin: DNS points the name to your server. nginx handles HTTPS (Let's Encrypt) and proxies to Node.
Pass the visitor address in headers and set `trust proxy`.
pm2 keeps the app running, restarts it after a crash and after a reboot.
Settings live in the server's `.env`, never in Git.
A repeatable deploy script: pull, install, build, restart, then check `/api/health`.
Open only the ports you need (80 and 443).
mern-capstone-checklist-and-next-steps: Checklist: secrets, ownership checks, validation, tests, backups, monitoring.
A committed secret stays in Git history. Check it and change the secret.
Deploy, then write a README with screenshots.
Pick one idea from the next-steps list and build it with a test.
Small, finished and deployed projects teach more than unfinished big ones.
